title: Running autonomous AI agents safely with OpenShell
excerpt: OpenShell isolates agents in a sandbox and enforces per-agent policies with kernel checks and formal verification.
body:
A recent release of OpenShell added kernel-level enforcement primitives and a formal verification step for policy changes. The runtime lets autonomous agents read files, install packages, call APIs and use credentials, but it never hands those secrets directly to the agent. Instead, a policy declares what each agent may touch and the system enforces that declaration at the operating-system level.

The post walks through three concrete pieces of the design, kernel enforcement, formal verification, and the extensible sandbox lifecycle, then ends with a single actionable takeaway.

## Kernel-level enforcement isolates file and network access

OpenShell runs every agent inside an isolated sandbox. The kernel is instrumented so that each file access, system call and outbound network connection is checked against the declared policy before it is allowed. Because the check happens inside the kernel, the agent cannot bypass it with user-space tricks.

The enforcement works for both files and network sockets. When an agent tries to open a path that is not listed in its filesystem rule, the kernel returns an error immediately.

Likewise, any `connect()` call is intercepted; the policy must contain an approved host and, if credentials are required, the gateway injects them only for that endpoint. The result is that agents see a virtual view of the filesystem and a filtered network stack, while the host’s real data and secrets stay untouched.

A quick way to try the sandbox is to run the installer and create a demo sandbox:

```
curl -LsSf https://raw.githubusercontent.com/NVIDIA/OpenShell/main/install.sh | sh
openshell sandbox create --name demo
```

The installer sets up the CLI and a local gateway, and the created sandbox uses a minimal Ubuntu image with no agent pre-installed. From that point, policies can be attached to the sandbox to grant or deny specific file paths or network hosts.

## Formal verification flags risky policy changes

Policy updates are not applied blindly. Before a change is accepted, OpenShell runs a formal verification pass that models the new policy and looks for risky expansions. The verifier flags any addition that would let an agent reach a new host with credentials, call a new API method, or otherwise broaden its attack surface.

The flagging is deterministic: the verifier produces a list of “risky new accesses” that must be reviewed by a human before the policy is committed. This step prevents accidental privilege escalation that could happen when a developer adds a new rule without fully understanding its implications. The source notes that the verifier works on both filesystem and network rules, ensuring that a change to one does not unintentionally open a hole in the other.

Because the verification happens before the policy is loaded into the kernel, the system never enforces a rule that has not been vetted. This two-stage guard, static analysis followed by runtime kernel checks, creates a defense-in-depth posture for autonomous agents that need to interact with external resources.

## Extensible sandbox lifecycle and provider model

OpenShell’s architecture separates the gateway, supervisor and sandbox, allowing each component to be swapped or extended. Sandboxes are defined by images, runtimes and optional GPU access, and they follow a clear lifecycle: creation, policy attachment, agent execution and teardown. The default image is a stripped-down Ubuntu base, but developers can supply custom images that include specific libraries or tools.

Providers are another extensible piece. A provider bundles credentials that are only exposed to approved endpoints. When an agent issues a request to a host listed in its network policy, the gateway injects the matching credential just for that request. The credential never appears on the filesystem, and it cannot be reused elsewhere.

The runtime also supports middleware, interceptors and compute drivers, making it possible to add logging, tracing or custom resource limits without modifying the core sandbox code. For Kubernetes deployments, the gateway can be installed with Helm and the cluster’s CNI must enforce a NetworkPolicy, ensuring that the same isolation guarantees hold at scale.

## The takeaway

OpenShell combines kernel-level enforcement with pre-flight formal verification, so agents get the capabilities they need without ever seeing unrestricted data or network access. Use the provided installer and `openshell sandbox create --name demo` command to spin up a sandbox, then attach a vetted policy before running any autonomous workload. This approach keeps the runtime safe while still letting agents perform useful actions.
